title: Why India's market crashed in March, then jumped in April
one_idea: Foreign selling accompanied the March fall, domestic buying buffered it, and April's rebound came from news and valuations while foreign funds kept selling.
audience_misconception: Foreign money alone decides whether the Indian market crashes or recovers.

claims.claim: In March 2026 foreign portfolio investors net sold a record ₹1,17,775 crore of Indian equities.
The Nifty 50 fell 9.37% in March 2026 (25,179 to 22,819.60, close to close), its steepest monthly fall since March 2020.

In April 2026 the Nifty rose 7.46%, its best month since December 2023; after a sharp sell-off triggered by the US-Iran war in March, a mid-April ceasefire, cheaper valuations and a steady earnings season helped markets rebound even as FIIs kept selling heavily.
FPIs withdrew about ₹60,847 crore in April 2026.
SEBI's monthly bulletin says that during March 2026 DIIs were net buyers in the equity segment with net inflows of ₹1,43,169 crore and acted as a critical buffer against FPI outflows.
FIIs are large global funds investing in India; DIIs are primarily Indian mutual funds, insurance companies and pension funds.
FIIs sold ₹44,013 crore of Indian equities in September 2026 while DIIs bought ₹76,030 crore.
On 5 October 2026 FIIs net sold ₹4,699.14 crore and DIIs net bought ₹5,181.62 crore (NSE capital market data).
Going long means buying a futures contract expecting the price to rise; going short means selling one expecting the price to fall.
A put option becomes more valuable as the underlying asset's price decreases.
The seller of a call option profits from the premium if the price drops below the strike price at expiration.
On 1 October 2026 FII index futures were 29,605 long and 339,779 short; index calls 670,483 long and 1,101,948 short; index puts 1,114,773 long and 448,195 short (contracts).

mechanism.step: Foreign funds sold a record ₹1.17 lakh crore of Indian shares in March 2026.
DIIs bought ₹1.43 lakh crore of equities in March, which SEBI called a critical buffer against the foreign outflow.
A buffer is not a floor: DIIs bought more than foreign funds sold, yet the Nifty still fell 9.37%.
The April rebound followed a ceasefire, cheaper valuations and steady earnings while foreign funds kept selling.
Flows in September and on 5 October show the same opposing pattern: foreign funds sell, domestic funds buy.

scenes.intent: The viewer is curious about a puzzle: a crash and a rebound that do not seem to fit together.

scenes.narration: In March, foreign investors pulled a record ₹1.17 lakh crore out of Indian stocks.

visual.label: pulled out by foreign investors, March 2026 (a record)

scenes.intent: The viewer sees how large the foreign exit was before any explanation is offered.

scenes.narration: The Nifty, India's main share index, fell over 9%: its worst month since the COVID crash.

visual.label: Nifty 50, March 2026: worst month since March 2020

scenes.intent: The viewer registers that the crash was real and severe, not a small dip.

scenes.narration: In April the Nifty jumped 7.5%, its best month in 28 months. Foreign investors still sold about ₹61,000 crore.

visual.label: Nifty 50, April 2026, while foreign investors still sold ₹60,847 crore

scenes.intent: The viewer is stuck on the puzzle: the market rose while foreign money kept leaving.

scenes.narration: Foreign funds are called FIIs. Indian mutual funds, insurers and pension funds are called DIIs.
scenes.intent: The viewer can name the two sides before the story continues.

scenes.narration: When foreign funds sold in March, DIIs bought ₹1.43 lakh crore. SEBI called it a critical buffer.
scenes.intent: The viewer sees the other side of the trade: domestic institutions absorbing what foreigners sold.

scenes.narration: A buffer does not stop a fall. DIIs bought more than foreign funds sold, yet the Nifty fell over 9%.
scenes.intent: The viewer learns the limit: domestic buying softens a fall but does not prevent it.

scenes.narration: April's rebound followed a US–Iran ceasefire, cheaper valuations and steady earnings. Foreign funds kept selling.
scenes.intent: The viewer gets the answer: the rebound came from news and valuations, not from foreign money returning.

scenes.narration: In September, foreign funds sold about ₹44,000 crore and domestic funds bought about ₹76,000 crore.
scenes.intent: The viewer sees the same opposing pattern in the latest data, up to this week.

scenes.narration: Foreign funds also trade derivatives. A long futures position bets on a rise; a short bets on a fall.

steps: Long: expects the price to rise

scenes.narration: On 1 October, foreign funds held about 310,000 more short than long index futures contracts.

visual.label: FII index futures net position, 1 Oct 2026 (short 339,779, long 29,605)

scenes.intent: The viewer learns what foreign funds hold in derivatives, in plain contract counts.

scenes.narration: Their options leaned the same way: more short calls, more long puts. Both benefit if the index falls.
scenes.intent: The viewer sees the options positions as numbers and which way they lean, with no claim about what they cause.

scenes.narration: In March a shock started the fall. DIIs buffered it. Send this to the friend who tracks FII flows.

steps: A US–Iran war shock started March's fall

scenes.intent: The viewer leaves with the three-part pattern from 2026 and someone to send it to.

director_notes:
ASSUME: audience curious_adult, format why_is_x with extra beats; story chosen by the owner: FII vs DII opposing forces, hook 'why the market crashes then goes up'.
RULING: March Nifty fall is spoken as 'more than 9%'. Sources disagree on the measure (9.37% close to close at Finnovate; 'more than 11%' at Outlook Money).
RULING: April FPI selling uses ₹60,847 crore (Ventura, NSDL-based). Dhan reports 'over ₹70,000 crore' from a different dataset; not used.
RULING: March DII buying uses SEBI's bulletin figure (₹1,43,169 crore, p.12). Other sources range from ₹1.26 to ₹1.95 lakh crore depending on what they count; the SEBI PDF cannot be read by the pipeline's page reader, so that claim was checked by hand (text extracted with pypdf).
RULING: no claim that FIIs' futures positions amplify or cause moves. NSE data shows FIIs net short index futures, which contradicts a margin-call amplification story (see ep22 review).
DEVIATE: the NSE flows URL (api/fiidiiTradeReact) returns only the latest day, so its 5 October figures will change; the same figures are shown on nseindia.com/reports/fii-dii for that date.
RULING: derivatives scenes state positions as contract counts only; no causal claim.
